analysis.one_liner: Lets consumers lock and control their credit bureau data free of charge.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Equifax data breach, this bill would have required the big credit reporting agencies to give every consumer a free, simple way to lock down their file so no one can pull their credit report without permission. It would have cut off the sale of consumer data for credit and insurance offers the consumer never asked for, extended fraud alerts to 10 years, let consumers get free copies of everything the agencies hold on them, and given active-duty military members extra protection. The Senate Banking Committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially people worried about identity theft after major breaches. Anyone could freeze or lock their credit file at no cost, stop the agencies from handing their data to third parties for credit and insurance pitches they never initiated, place a 10-year fraud alert with a simple statement of suspicion rather than a police report, and get free reports covering information held by affiliates of the bureaus. Active-duty military would get active-duty alerts plus free, fast access to their files.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each major credit reporting agency to give consumers a secure, convenient, cost-free method to release or block the release of any information in their file for credit, insurance, or opening financial accounts [S3].

Bars agencies from providing consumer information to third parties for credit or insurance transactions the consumer did not initiate, and blocks the lock tool itself from being used to collect or market data [S2] [S3].

Extends fraud alerts from 7 years to 10, lets consumers claim one by asserting a good-faith suspicion of fraud or a data breach instead of filing an identity theft report, and allows renewal in further 10-year periods [S3].

Gives consumers free access to their file without regard to whether the information is held by a parent, subsidiary, or affiliate of the agency, and removes the once-per-12-months limit on free disclosures [S3].
Expands protections for active-duty military consumers, including notice of free file access and delivery of required disclosures within 3 business days at no charge [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three major credit reporting agencies — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — plus data brokers and marketers who buy bureau data. The bill ends their ability to sell consumer files for credit and insurance offers consumers never requested, takes away fees for locks and extra file access, and requires them to build and run the free lock system. Lenders and insurers that rely on prescreened prospect lists would lose that pipeline.

drawbacks.text: Restricting bureau data sharing to consumer-initiated transactions could make legitimate credit and insurance shopping less seamless, since prescreened firm offers would shrink [S2].
The bureaus would bear the cost of building and operating the free lock system and longer alert services, an expense that could show up in their other pricing [S3].
The bill relies on the consumer to affirmatively lock their file; it does not default everyone to locked, so protection still depends on consumers learning about and using the tool [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the benefits are large and direct: free control over who can see their credit file, longer fraud alerts, and fuller free access to their own data, all aimed at a real harm — identity theft after breaches like Equifax's. The costs fall almost entirely on the bureaus and data marketers, whose business model depends on selling consumer information. The main honest criticism is that the bill puts the burden on consumers to act rather than locking files by default, so its protection is only as good as consumer awareness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on February 5, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1] [S5].
The bill received no further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit reporting agencies and data marketers: because the bill died, they keep selling consumer files for credit and insurance pitches and charging for services like locks and extra file access that the bill would have made free.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee; recruited no cosponsors before it stalled.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, which sat untouched from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic senator introduced the bill, no Republican or other member cosponsored it, and a Republican-led committee declined to move it; the record shows a fully partisan split by inaction rather than by any vote.

industries.note: Their business is collecting consumer files and selling access; free locks, limits on third-party sharing, and free affiliate-file disclosure would cut directly into that revenue. The bill is literally named after Equifax's 2017 breach.
They lose the flow of bureau data used to prescreen consumers for credit and insurance offers the consumers never requested.

industries.industry: Lenders and insurers using prescreened offers
industries.note: They lose prescreened prospect lists for offers consumers did not initiate, but keep full access for transactions consumers actually start. The effect on them is narrower than on the bureaus themselves.
